clue.text: Controversial candidate wanting power … and nearly becoming president?

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter for power is dropped from the candidate

parts.note: Donald Trump, a divisive candidate for the White House when this puzzle appeared
P is the standard abbreviation for power in physics

indicators.note: nearly says the word and is cut short by its final letter

explanation.surface: A commentator mutters about a divisive candidate who, minus a bit of power, almost reaches the presidency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting power' takes P from TRUMP; 'nearly' trims AND to AN. 'Becoming' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Truman was the thirty-third holder of the American presidency, so he is an example of a president.

clue.text: Material upset big cheese

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word reads upwards

parts.note: fat means big
feta is a Greek cheese

explanation.surface: A fabric has offended the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big cheese' looks like one phrase meaning boss; it is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Taffeta is a crisp woven silk fabric, an example of material.

clue.text: Extreme skill? Partly luck, on reflection

indicators.note: on reflection means mirrored, so the pieces read backwards

parts.note: art means skill, as in the art of conversation

indicators.note: partly says only some of the word luck is used

explanation.surface: Is it really great skill, or partly luck, when you think about it?
explanation.walkthrough: ART plus LU (part of luck) is reversed by 'on reflection'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultra as an adjective means extreme, especially of political views.

clue.text: Group heading off to fish for sport

indicators.note: heading off says the first letter is removed

parts.note: a gang is a group
ling is a fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A club party sets off to fish for fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Angling is fishing with rod and line, practised as a sport or pastime.

clue.text: Call on setter to retire — it makes you sick!

indicators.note: to retire is to go back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: to cite is to call or summon, for instance a witness
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: The solver wants the setter to step down, since the puzzle is nauseating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is only a link; 'to retire' reverses the whole call-plus-setter string.
explanation.definitionFit: An emetic is a substance that induces vomiting, which is a description of the substance's effect.

clue.text: China's quite regularly embraced change

indicators.note: embraced means held inside, so the picked letters go within

parts.note: china is rhyming slang for mate (china plate); the 's is a link

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter of quite

explanation.surface: The Chinese state has fairly steadily welcomed reform.
explanation.walkthrough: China is Cockney rhyming slang: china plate = mate. 'Regularly' picks UT from quite.
explanation.definitionFit: To mutate is to change form, a near synonym.

clue.text: Wrong people arrested for eliminating female bully

indicators.note: arrested means held captive, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
men means people, as in an army's men

indicators.note: eliminating says the female letter is removed from the word for

explanation.surface: Men wrongly arrested in place of a woman who was the real bully.
explanation.definitionFit: A tormentor torments victims, behaviour typical of a bully.

clue.text: Brought round to prepare, regularly, a cold meal for queen

indicators.note: brought round means turned around, so the pieces read upwards

parts.note: to do food is to prepare it, as in do the vegetables
oft means often, i.e. regularly
C is the abbreviation for cold on taps

explanation.surface: A cold dish is regularly brought round for the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen' is a female cat, not royalty. 'To' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A queen is a female cat, and her meal is cat food: a cryptic sense of the definition.

clue.text: Our own dear land

parts.note: dear means expensive, so the phrase suggests a country where everything costs too much

explanation.surface: A patriotic line about a beloved homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' reads as beloved but means expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Overcharging is called a rip-off, and Britain is the speaker's own country, notorious for high prices.

clue.text: Draw fellow in back as means of identification

indicators.note: back says the combined letters are read in the reverse direction
in places the fellow's letter inside the draw

parts.note: a tie is a drawn match
F is the abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS

explanation.surface: An artist sketches a man in the background so he can be identified later.
explanation.walkthrough: F goes inside TIE to make TIFE, which 'back' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: An E-fit is a computer-built likeness of a suspect's face used by police to identify someone.

clue.text: Glamorous people I follow around (and refuse to stop)

indicators.note: to stop is to plug a gap, so the rubbish word goes into the middle
around says the letters of I and the follow word are turned back to front

parts.note: to tag along is to follow, so tag means follow
refuse as a noun is rubbish, i.e. litter

explanation.surface: Someone trails after the beautiful people but won't stop to tidy up after them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' is a noun, not the verb its brackets suggest. 'Around' gives GATI, and 'to stop' plugs the rubbish into its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: The glitterati are fashionable celebrities, a collective term for glamorous society people.

clue.text: Language needing clarification — plain English!

indicators.note: words needing clarification are muddled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tongue so muddled it needs plain English to make sense of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing clarification' rearranges PLAIN plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: Nepali is the official tongue of Nepal, an example of a language.

clue.text: Doctor not male — one patient at it

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters of not are shuffled

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
Job of the Bible is proverbial for his patience

explanation.surface: A female doctor and a patient are, it seems, getting up to something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' rearranges NOT to ONT. The 'patience of Job' is a stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at it and being on the job both mean busily working, and both are slang for having sex.

clue.text: Taking part in tiebreaker hasn't lost — it's working

indicators.note: hasn't says the letter for lost is missing

parts.note: a playoff decides a tie, so its players are playing off
L is the abbreviation for lost in league tables

explanation.surface: A competitor in a tiebreaker is still in it, so the effort is working.
explanation.definitionFit: A plan that pays off succeeds, so paying off means working out well.

clue.text: Suggests it's raised among prisoners

indicators.note: among places the turned word inside the prisoners

parts.note: inmates are prisoners

indicators.note: raised in a down clue means lifted, so the word reads upwards

parts.note: it, the 's being is as a link

explanation.surface: Someone hints that the matter has come up among the convicts.
explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to hint or imply, so suggests is a synonym.

clue.text: Boss's room not quite finished

indicators.note: not quite finished says the room word loses its final letter

parts.note: a study is a room for reading and work

explanation.surface: The manager's office is still being fitted out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' here is not a manager but a raised knob; the 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is an ornamental knob or projection, and a stud is a similar raised button or rivet.

clue.text: Cash from court gets Henry on track

parts.note: Pat Cash, the Australian Wimbledon tennis champion
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Money awarded by a judge sets Henry back on course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cash' is not money but tennis player Pat Cash, of the court.
explanation.definitionFit: A path is a track or way to walk along, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Liberal academic finds employment

parts.note: a prof is a professor, an academic
use means employment, as in the employment of force

explanation.surface: A left-leaning don lands a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' looks political but means generous.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal can mean lavish or plentiful, as in a liberal helping, which is what profuse means.

clue.text: Sign to west, proper elections

indicators.note: to west says the proper word sits to the left of the sign, in an across clue

parts.note: prim means proper or prudish
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A signpost pointing west and a proper vote, as if out of a campaign trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Primaries are preliminary elections in which party candidates are chosen, especially in the US.

clue.text: Poet (old woman) cut very complicated lines

parts.note: ma is mother, informally the old woman

indicators.note: complicated means tangled up, so the shortened letters are rearranged
cut says the word very loses its last letter

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for line, so LL is lines

explanation.surface: A poet's mother edited some very convoluted verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' trims very to VER and 'complicated' rearranges it to RVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Marvell was a 17th-century English metaphysical poet.

clue.text: Was son left outside?

indicators.note: outside says the left word goes around the son

parts.note: exited means left, as in went out
S is the abbreviation for son in genealogies

explanation.surface: A question of whether the boy was shut out of the house.
explanation.definitionFit: Existed means lived or was, so the two are synonyms of being.

clue.text: Quickly aware of pair on top

indicators.note: on top in a down clue puts the pair abbreviation above the rest

parts.note: to be onto something is to be aware of it

explanation.surface: Someone swiftly learns of a couple getting the upper hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronto is informal for immediately, so quickly is its synonym.

clue.text: Claptrap from Conservative members occasionally worth recalling

indicators.note: recalling is calling back, so the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: a Tory is a British Conservative
M is an abbreviation for member, so two of them make members

indicators.note: occasionally takes every other letter of worth

explanation.surface: Nonsense from Tory MPs that is only now and then worth remembering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' picks OT from worth; 'recalling' reverses TORYMMOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Claptrap and tommyrot are both informal words for nonsense or empty talk.

clue.text: Instructions to massage deep, not hard

parts.note: to rub is to massage

indicators.note: not says the letter for hard is removed

parts.note: rich means deep, of a colour or sound
H is the abbreviation for hard on pencils

explanation.surface: Directions for a masseur: press deeply but not too firmly.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubric is a heading of directions, such as the instructions on an exam paper.

clue.text: Horse nibbling Mr Turner's nuts

indicators.note: nibbling means holding in the mouth, so the horse goes around the title

parts.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse

indicators.note: a turner turns things round, so its work reverses the title

explanation.surface: A horse munches on the nuts belonging to a Mr Turner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turner' looks like the painter but is a reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is British slang for crazy, and nuts is another slang word for mad.

clue.text: Rose sportingly let out after retraction at the last minute

parts.note: Justin Rose is an English golfer

indicators.note: after retraction means once drawn back, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: to emit is to let out

explanation.surface: A rose, played with in a sport, is released after being drawn back in the nick of time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' is golfer Justin Rose, not a flower or 'got up'; 'retraction' reverses EMIT to TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something just in time means doing it only just before a deadline, at the last possible moment.

clue.text: Eight organisations rejected features writer

indicators.note: rejected says the hidden letters are read backwards
features means contains as a part, so the run is inside the two clue words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Eight bodies turn down a journalist who writes feature articles.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'features writer' as the definition, leaving the hidden word without an indicator. 'Features' is that indicator (the phrase contains the letters), and 'writer' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Roth was an American novelist, an example of a writer.

clue.text: Refrain from taking action over training centre?

indicators.note: over says the phrase is turned over, reading backwards

parts.note: to refrain from taking legal action is to not sue

explanation.surface: A sports academy decides against legal action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking action' looks general but means suing. Euston is a major London railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus is a hub for trains, so a train centre is a punning sense of training centre.

clue.text: Holder and others sounded greatly impressed

indicators.note: sounded says the band name is said aloud

parts.note: Noddy Holder was lead singer of the British glam rock band Slade

explanation.surface: A cup holder and others made a noise, much impressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holder' is Noddy Holder, singer of the 1970s British glam rock band Slade.
explanation.definitionFit: Slayed is slang for overwhelmed or wowed an audience, so to be greatly impressed.
